articles.title: Stanford prison experiment: why do controversial psychology studies still have such a hold on us?
articles.author: David Kaposi, Psychotherapist and Senior Lecturer in Psychology, The Open University
paras: Two of the most famous experiments in psychology, the Stanford prison experiment and Stanley Milgram’s obedience studies, have been called a sham, a lie and a fraud.

Retraction Watch, a site that tracks withdrawn research papers, has hosted an argument for retracting the Stanford paper. Psychologists have even been told that almost everything they thought they knew about Milgram is wrong.

Yet interest has not faded. This month, Netflix released six episodes of The New Stanford Prison Experiment, putting the 1971 study back in the spotlight. Why do these much-criticised experiments keep drawing us back?

Part of the answer is how strong the original findings sounded. They came from what is often called the golden age of American social psychology, roughly the 1950s to the early 1970s. Researchers in this period ran dramatic experiments on how groups and authority shape what ordinary people do.

In the 1950s, the psychologist Solomon Asch asked students to match the length of a line to one of three others. When a room of actors all gave the same wrong answer, many of the real participants went along with them – at least some of the time.

In the early 1960s at Yale University, Stanley Milgram told volunteers they were helping with a study of memory and learning. They were asked to give electric shocks – rising to a level labelled dangerous – to a man in another room whenever he got a question wrong.

The shocks were fake and the man was an actor, but the participants did not know that. In the experiment’s initial version, 65% of them went all the way to the top of the scale when a man in a lab coat told them to continue.

In the late 1960s, the psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané studied why people so often fail to help in an emergency. In one experiment, volunteers heard over an intercom what sounded like another participant having a seizure. The more people they believed could also hear, the less likely each one was to go for help.

Philip Zimbardo, a Stanford University psychologist who later became president of the American Psychological Association, was the last of these big names. In August 1971, he turned the basement of Stanford’s psychology department into a mock prison. He randomly assigned 24 male students to play guards or prisoners in what was meant to be a two-week study.
He had to stop it after just six days, however, because some of the guards had become overly cruel and some of the prisoners had broken down.

In a 2019 analysis of the Stanford archive, the French researcher Thibault Le Texier argued that Zimbardo’s team gave the guards instructions on how to behave, so they were not acting spontaneously. Some prisoners later said they had exaggerated their distress. The study also began as a student project.

Milgram’s work has also been attacked. One analysis argued that he manufactured obedience in the lab rather than discovered it. And psychologists, writing for The Conversation, have pointed out that across all versions of his experiment, more people disobeyed than obeyed.

Some of this criticism, though, is not new, because the researchers disclosed the facts themselves. Zimbardo’s 2007 bestseller, The Lucifer Effect, credits his students with the original idea. It also describes how he acted as the prison’s “superintendent” and briefed and coached the guards.

The same goes for Milgram. He published the results of many of the variations himself, and noted that obedience fell sharply in some of them. However, those were variations that bore little resemblance to the original experiment setup.

The harder test is the alternative explanation. Alex Haslam of the University of Queensland and Stephen Reicher of the University of St Andrews, both social psychologists, have argued for years that obedience alone cannot explain what happened. In 2002, they ran the BBC prison study, a televised re-run of Zimbardo’s idea, in which guards did not spontaneously turn cruel.

They suggest that participants believed in the scientific cause and chose to carry on – an idea they call “engaged followership”. Their explanation has numerous critics, however, who say they overlook evidence from what was said and done during Milgram’s and Zimbardo’s original sessions.

Flawed though their experiments may have been by today’s ethical and methodological standards, Zimbardo and Milgram did chance upon something grave and important in human nature. They confronted their participants with a clear moral dilemma: will you choose evil, or will you choose good? And they witnessed ordinary person after ordinary person freely – albeit agonisingly – choosing evil.
That profound and deeply disturbing message is why people keep coming back to these decades-old studies.

Nothing that Zimbardo, Milgram, their most committed supporters or their fiercest critics have said comes close to fully explaining why ordinary people in their labs tended to choose evil when they could, with no consequence, choose good.

Of course, many of the pressures that made that fateful choice difficult are now known. But no amount of pressure accounts for the Stanford guards choosing to brutalise their fellows, or Milgram’s participants choosing to give yet another electric shock, when they could have freely chosen otherwise.

Zimbardo, Milgram and the other studies reveal something monstrous about ordinary human beings – about us all – while remaining elusive, enigmatic, almost mysterious. Until we understand why, as Milgram’s experimenter told hesitant participants: “The experiment requires that you continue.”

articles.title: Tired, irritable and craving carbs? Why darker days affect our bodies and brains
articles.author: Laurence Wainwright, Departmental Lecturer and Course Director, Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment, University of Oxford
paras: When the clocks go back in October, millions of Britons welcome an extra hour in bed. But by the evening, with darkness arriving before many people finish work, that small luxury may seem a distant memory.

As autumn turns into winter, you might feel unusually tired, struggle to concentrate, or crave carbohydrate-rich comfort foods. Getting out of bed becomes harder, while a night on the sofa seems more appealing than going out.
It’s tempting to dismiss this as the winter blues. But shorter days can influence our sleep and mood.

The clock change, which also happens in many other countries, doesn’t reduce daylight. It shifts an hour of it from evening to morning. However, it coincides with shortening days, when some people struggle to get enough natural light.
For around 3% of the UK population, winter brings a form of depression known as seasonal affective disorder (SAD).

People with SAD experience recurring depressive episodes, usually beginning in autumn or winter and improving in spring. Symptoms include persistent low mood, irritability, difficulty concentrating and losing interest in enjoyable activities. It can also involve sleeping more, increased appetite and cravings for carbohydrates.

These symptoms can affect work and relationships. Other people experience milder seasonal changes without meeting the criteria for clinical depression, while some notice changes in sleep but little difference in mood.
What happens to our body clocks?

Our circadian system, or internal body clock, helps regulate when we feel alert and sleepy. Light-sensitive cells in the retina detect environmental light and signal to the brain’s central clock. This helps coordinate daily rhythms, including the release of melatonin, a hormone involved in sleep.

Bright morning daylight helps synchronise that clock with the outside world. But someone who travels to work before sunrise, spends the day indoors, and returns after sunset may get relatively little natural light. Even on cloudy days, outdoor light is generally much brighter than typical office lighting.
Reduced daylight exposure can affect circadian timing and may contribute to seasonal changes in sleep and mood, although the mechanisms behind SAD aren’t fully understood.

Research also suggests our sleep varies with the seasons. A 2025 study of sleep-tracking data from more than 116,000 adults found that people in the northern hemisphere slept approximately 15 to 20 minutes longer in winter than summer. These differences persisted despite artificial lighting and relatively fixed working hours.
Does turning the clocks back make matters worse? The evidence is mixed.

A Danish study reported more hospital contacts for depression following the autumn change. However, a 2025 study in England found fewer recorded depression-related health events in the following week. The studies measured different outcomes; neither proves that changing the clocks causes seasonal depression.
An ancient biological response?

Evolutionary biology offers one possible explanation for winter lethargy. For our ancestors in temperate climates, winter brought colder conditions and less predictable food supplies. Searching for food in harsh weather could be risky, so conserving energy might have offered a survival advantage.
Researchers have proposed that the increased sleep, appetite and weight gain associated with some cases of seasonal depression reflect an inherited tendency to conserve energy when food is scarce.
It’s an intriguing hypothesis, but difficult to test. We cannot conclude that modern humans have an automatic, evolutionarily programmed slowdown in metabolism whenever daylight declines.

Seasonal depression is complex, with genetic susceptibility, circadian rhythms and environmental circumstances potentially contributing. Nevertheless, our sensitivity to seasonal light raises questions about modern working life. Most workplaces expect similar productivity throughout the year, even though opportunities to spend time outdoors can differ considerably between July and November.

There are practical steps that may help. The NHS recommends getting outside during daylight, exercising regularly and keeping consistent sleeping and waking times. Staying connected with other people can also help.

For SAD, treatment options include cognitive behavioural therapy and antidepressants. Research on particular medicines needs careful interpretation. A small study involving 37 patients suggested that agomelatine might improve symptoms, while a Cochrane review found that bupropion could help prevent recurrence in people with a history of winter depression. The latter evidence doesn’t establish its effectiveness for treating an episode already underway.
Bright-light therapy may also help some people, although NICE says evidence of its effectiveness remains uncertain.

Anyone experiencing persistent depressive symptoms should speak to a GP rather than assuming they’re simply tired because it’s winter. Workplaces could help too, by making it easier for staff to spend time outdoors during daylight.
As the evenings draw in, recognising the biological influences on mood and energy may help us respond more effectively, without expecting another coffee to solve everything.

articles.title: Five ways to look after yourself as winter approaches
articles.author: Andy M Morley, Subject Lead: Psychology & Neuroscience, University of Lancashire
paras: When the clocks “fall back” in the autumn, it signals the start of the winter months. And, for many, this time change also signals the start of a difficult period – where the cold weather and long nights wear on their mental health.
To help you adjust to the darker evenings, here are our five top tips for easing your way through the winter:
1. Make the most of the daylight

Natural light regulates our body clock – the internal system which influences our sleep quality and alertness. Your body will take time to adjust to the changes, notably the evenings being darker, earlier. This in turn may disrupt your sleep patterns, which might mean grumpier mornings due to a lack of sleep.

Try to make the most of the day’s light by spending time outdoors – even if this is just a walk around the block during your lunch or while on a coffee break. A change of scenery can offer a welcome pause from the pressures of everyday life and help you feel refreshed, particularly if you focus on the greenery around you.
Even if you cannot find time to leave the building, try sitting next by a window to enjoy some natural light and a different perspective on you surroundings.
When it’s cold and dark, it’s all too easy to skip your workouts and hunker down inside with a hot drink or favourite snack instead.
But exercise has many benefits for us beyond just the physical ones. It can reduce stress and improve your mental health.

Taking a stroll, visiting the gym or even walking laps around your kitchen table or garden will help you cope with the change in the season. You could even combine exercise with seasonal activities – such as walking to see Halloween decorations or Christmas lights in the local area.

It’s perfectly okay to adjust your expectations about your daily accomplishments in the winter months. With less daylight and worsening weather it can be hard to keep to the pace of life you’ve set yourself and enjoyed over the summer months.
Self-compassion supports your wellbeing. This can involve being kind to yourself, recognising the things you have achieved and celebrating the small wins along the way.

You don’t have to make the most of everyday, or be productive all of the time. Find the balance and allow yourself some slower days. And rather than criticising yourself for not completing everything you had lined up for the day, acknowledge what you have achieved. Having this kind of self-compassion is linked with better mental wellbeing.
4. Stay connected to others

When it’s dark, cold and wet, it’s easy to want to prioritise “me time” at the expense of catching up. But making time for your friends and family is key during the winter months. This is because strong social connections are important for good mental health.

Even if it’s just a short chat about a new film you’ve seen or a great book you’ve read, this time spent connecting with loved ones and maintaining these meaningful connections can help to support your mental wellbeing.
5. Enjoy life’s simple pleasures
Make time for the little things in life – whether that’s reading, cooking, listening to music or picking up a hobby you forgot about.
Research on behavioural activation, which involves reconnecting with rewarding and meaningful activities, shows that these kinds of endeavours improve mood – particularly when motivation has fallen.

Planning one “fun” thing to do each day – no matter how big or small – can help ease the darker evenings and colder nights. You can also make the most of the longer evenings by snuggling up under the duvet to watch a box set without feeling you have to make the most of being outside, or enjoy more at-home activities – such as cooking a favourite meal or indulging in seasonal treats.
If nothing else, remember the shortest day of the year (in the UK at least) is only a few weeks away. After that, the evenings will start to get lighter again.

Looking after your mental health during winter isn’t about forcing yourself to be positive – it’s about finding the small ways that provide you with support, happiness or enable you to connect with other people.

Feeling less energetic during the winter is common, but if you have persistent low mood, a loss of interest in activities, feel hopeless or loss your appetite, seek additional support via the NHS. Self-care is important, but you do not have to manage everything alone.

articles.title: Greener maternity care starts with changing hospitals, without putting pressure on pregnant women
articles.author: Alice Craggs, Lecturer in Midwifery, School of Nursing and Midwifery, London South Bank University
paras: The NHS has a substantial carbon footprint. Yet one part of its environmental impact receives relatively little attention: maternity care.

The health service is responsible for an estimated 4% to 5% of England’s greenhouse gas emissions. A 2025 report from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists estimated that selected maternity care activities in England generated about 205,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) in 2022–23.

CO₂e expresses the warming effect of different greenhouse gases, such as methane, as an equivalent amount of carbon dioxide. The analysis excluded some maternity services, so the total footprint is likely to be higher.

Nearly 29% of the emissions across the activities studied came from Entonox, commonly known as gas and air. It contains nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. Using it during regular contractions over four hours has an estimated warming effect of 237kg CO₂e.

Travel to appointments also contributes to emissions. An analysis at the Whittington, a hospital in north London, estimated that a patient’s return journey to an antenatal appointment generated an average of 1.23kg CO₂e.
Hospitals also use large quantities of disposable equipment. Ready-to-use formula bottles and teats, single-use cups and clinical waste containers are routinely used once and discarded.

Pregnancy is sometimes described as a “teachable moment”, when people may be particularly receptive to health information. Environmental advice could become part of those conversations, including discussions about feeding a baby or choosing pain relief.
Responsibility for reducing emissions

But placing responsibility on parents creates ethical problems. Maternity care in the UK is already under intense pressure. The 2022 Ockenden review documented serious failures in maternity safety, while the 2024 birth trauma inquiry highlighted how women’s concerns were dismissed or ignored.
Against that background, asking someone in labour to weigh the climate effects of pain relief alongside their comfort and safety could create another burden at an already demanding time.

Measuring emissions can help hospitals improve how services are designed. But carbon targets should not be used to restrict access to caesarean birth or pain relief. Decisions about care should respect each person’s needs and informed choices.

In a small interview study involving 12 people who had used nitrous oxide during labour, most wanted environmental information to be available during pregnancy. However, they were unsure whether knowing its impact would change their choice of pain relief. Participants also considered reducing emissions to be primarily the responsibility of healthcare organisations.
A more useful approach is to change how maternity services are delivered while protecting patient choice.

Some NHS maternity services are already doing this. At Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals, a project introduced virtual ward support and care at home for patients with severe pregnancy sickness. By reducing hospital stays, it cut emissions by an estimated 538kg CO₂e over one month. The team projected an annual saving of around 6,462kg if those reductions continued.

Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust has introduced technology that captures exhaled gas and air and breaks down the nitrous oxide into nitrogen and oxygen, allowing women to continue using gas and air during labour while reducing its environmental impact.

Other changes involve purchasing and waste. Thousands of ready-to-use plastic formula bottles and teats are used in maternity care. A 2019 letter from Irish researchers published in the British Medical Journal highlighted waste from unconsumed formula and discarded packaging. Reducing this could lower emissions without restricting access to formula for those who need or choose it.

Similar questions apply to disposable products throughout maternity wards. Clinicians work in systems designed around single-use equipment and established waste procedures. Changing those systems is likely to be more effective than expecting individual clinicians to improvise greener alternatives.
At the midwife-led White Horse birth centre in Swindon, staff have replaced plastic containers used to dispose of placentas with alternatives made from 96% paper, reducing plastic use and costs.

Breastfeeding illustrates how complicated individual responsibility can become. Compared with exclusive formula feeding, exclusive breastfeeding for six months has been estimated to have a carbon footprint 95kg to 153kg CO₂e lower per baby.

But feeding decisions depend on health and personal circumstances, including the support available to parents. A more useful approach would be to provide effective support for anyone who wants to breastfeed, while reducing unnecessary waste and emissions from the way formula is purchased, prepared and supplied by maternity services.
Better care, lower emissions

The Green Maternity Challenge, part of a programme led by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, brought together nine NHS teams to test ways of reducing emissions while improving maternity care. Several projects involved redesigning services to make treatment easier to access or reduce unnecessary hospital stays.

Better care and lower emissions can go together. But treating sustainability only as a fortunate side effect risks overlooking opportunities to design maternity services deliberately around lower-carbon care.

Hospitals should examine where their emissions come from and give staff the knowledge and resources to reduce them. Changes to purchasing and waste systems, alongside suitable lower-emission technologies, can help services become greener while protecting safe care and informed choice.

Childbirth will always carry an environmental footprint. Health services have the responsibility and practical means to reduce the impact through changes to how care is organised and delivered. Those changes should protect choices without placing additional burdens on the person giving birth.

articles.title: Diagnostic uncertainty: why losing a diagnosis can be as difficult as receiving one
articles.author: Esca van Blarikom, Postdoctoral Researcher in Medical Anthropology, Department of Global Health & Social Medicine, King's College London
paras: When actor Christina Applegate revealed that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS), she described the experience as “very unnerving” and “really confusing”.
For five years, MS had provided an explanation for her symptoms. Now, although those symptoms remained, the diagnosis that had helped her make sense of them was gone.
“I haven’t gotten better… If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways,” she explained. She also described feeling that she had lost the “reason” that had helped her make sense of her daily struggles.

Being told you don’t have a disease might seem like good news. But for someone living with symptoms, losing a diagnosis can mean losing an explanation for their suffering, along with the hope that explanation provides.

My ethnographic research into the experiences of people living with multiple conditions helps explain why. Through interviews and observations, I explored how diagnoses shape people’s understanding of their symptoms, their expectations for treatment and their sense of what the future might hold.

One participant in my London-based study had spent years living with debilitating back pain, struggling to get out of bed in the morning. After tests and referrals, a rheumatologist suggested that her symptoms might have an inflammatory cause.

Although this was only a possible diagnosis, it changed how she understood her condition. The specialist introduced medical terms that helped her make sense of symptoms that seemed confusing and unpredictable.
For the first time, there appeared to be an explanation for her suffering. The possibility of identifying an inflammatory condition also offered hope of treatment and specialist care.
But that hope was short-lived. Weeks later, a scan showed no evidence of the suspected inflammation. She was discharged from the clinic without the answers she had hoped for.
Her symptoms had not disappeared, and in the months that followed, her mental health deteriorated markedly.

Unlike Applegate, this participant had never received a confirmed diagnosis that was subsequently withdrawn. But both experiences reveal how much can be invested in a medical explanation, even before it is established.
For the woman in my study, the disappointing test result meant losing a possible way forward after years of uncertainty.
How diagnoses can shape experience
A diagnosis can influence much more than the treatment someone receives. It can also change how they interpret their symptoms and what they expect from their illness.
Research suggests that the attention we pay to bodily sensations can influence how we experience and report them.

In a 2024 experimental study, researchers found that repeatedly asking people about their symptoms increased the number they reported. This effect was particularly pronounced among people with higher levels of health anxiety or existing symptom distress.

These findings do not mean that symptoms are imagined or caused by receiving a diagnosis. They suggest that our awareness and interpretation of bodily sensations can be influenced by the circumstances in which we experience them.
A diagnosis can also create new fears.
When Applegate first received her MS diagnosis, she spoke about experiencing a profound depression and feeling fatalistic about her future.
People with physical health conditions have an increased risk of depression, although this can reflect many factors, including the effects of illness itself.
Another participant in my research described how her quality of life deteriorated after receiving a diagnosis of a chronic condition.
Before the diagnosis, her symptoms had been difficult to interpret. Afterwards, she increasingly understood them as possible signs of deterioration.
She felt that her quality of life had declined significantly following the diagnosis, rather than simply after the onset of her symptoms.
This illustrates how receiving a medical explanation can alter someone’s expectations about their future, particularly when a condition is presented as chronic or difficult to treat.

Research on nocebo effects offers one possible insight into the relationship between expectations and symptoms. Experimental studies have shown that negative expectations can increase experiences of pain through psychological and physiological processes.

This does not establish that the diagnosis caused my participant’s deterioration. However, it helps illustrate why the expectations surrounding illness deserve attention alongside its physical effects.
What happens when the diagnosis disappears
A diagnosis can provide access to treatment, but it may also offer recognition, reassurance and a sense of belonging.

Applegate has spoken about finding support within the MS community. Losing her diagnosis therefore raised questions extending beyond her medical treatment, including her place within a community that had become important to her.
For people with persistent symptoms, the absence of a diagnosis can also create difficulties in having their experiences understood and taken seriously.
Researchers studying unexplained symptoms have highlighted the disadvantages people can face when they lack a shared explanation for what they are experiencing.
This is why a negative test result does not necessarily resolve a patient’s difficulties. It may rule out one possible cause while leaving the symptoms, and the need for care, unchanged.
The challenge for healthcare professionals is to communicate diagnostic uncertainty without leaving patients feeling abandoned.

A 2024 study of GP consultations found that doctors varied considerably in how they explained plans for managing uncertain diagnoses. Some offered detailed guidance, while others provided less information about what patients should do if symptoms persisted or worsened.

For patients who have lost a diagnosis, continuing care might involve explaining why the original diagnosis has changed, acknowledging the distress that this can cause and agreeing on the next steps for investigation or symptom management.
These conversations also need to recognise that ruling out a particular disease does not invalidate the symptoms someone continues to experience.

Applegate’s experience illustrates something important about the role diagnoses play in people’s lives. They can shape how we understand our bodies, our relationships with others and our expectations for the future.
When a diagnosis is withdrawn, those understandings may have to be rebuilt, even as the symptoms that prompted the original investigation continue.

For doctors, the responsibility does not end when a diagnosis is ruled out. Patients still need help making sense of what is happening to them, especially when medicine cannot yet provide a clear answer.

articles.title: Scientists aim to give lung cells a memory of how to fight viruses
articles.author: Salim Khakoo, Professor of Hepatology, University of Southampton
paras: Respiratory infections affect billions of people every year and are among the top five causes of death worldwide. Despite recent medical advances, viruses such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) can still cause severe and even fatal illness.
Milder infections, including the common cold, are usually not fatal. But the cold can be caused by many different viruses, and it leads to a lot of time off work and a heavy cost to the economy.
These infections hit some groups harder than others. People living in deprived areas, older people and very young children are more likely to become seriously ill or die.

A government-funded research project called Triumph-NK, based at the University of Southampton, aims to prevent that harm. Our team is working on a new kind of vaccine that could protect against a wide range of respiratory viruses and be used immediately in an outbreak or even a pandemic.
The project is part of a wider programme called “sustained viral resilience”. Its aim is to strengthen the body’s first line of defence, known as the innate immune system.

The immune system has two main parts: first responders (the innate system) and a second line of defence (the adaptive system). Current vaccines work through the adaptive system, which is precise but slow to get going, so a virus can keep spreading in the meantime.
These vaccines also have to be developed separately for each virus, which takes more time. The project hopes to get around both delays by targeting a type of immune cell called a natural killer cell.

Natural killer cells are among the first cells to respond to a viral infection. They recognise molecular flags on infected cells that signal danger, then destroy those cells, killing the viruses inside and stopping the infection from spreading through the body.

Cells and antibodies of the adaptive system are very precise, and usually recognise only one virus or even one strain of a virus. Natural killer cells can spot cells infected by a broad range of different viruses.
Until recently, scientists thought natural killer cells were short-lived. Over the past decade, research has shown that some can survive in the body for a long time.
These long-lived cells are known as memory natural killer cells. They respond faster to many different viruses, and they are found in the nose and lungs, where respiratory infections begin.

Triumph-NK aims to find new ways to program natural killer cells in the body to become memory natural killer cells. They would then act as gatekeepers for the nose and lungs, stopping viruses from entering the body.

The first step is to work out which type of memory natural killer cell is best suited to the job. Our team is studying natural killer cells in the nose and lungs using DNA and RNA sequencing, while also identifying the molecular flags on the surface of the lung natural killer cells.

Once these cells are clearly identified, we will test different ways of making them in the laboratory using a range of stimuli. When they find the right combination, we will design a vaccine to deliver those stimuli using the mRNA technology behind the COVID vaccines.

The vaccine will be tested in the lab against a broad range of viruses, including influenza, COVID and RSV. It will then need thorough testing before human studies, which we hope to begin within the next five years.

If the work succeeds, the result would be a cost-effective, off-the-shelf vaccine that protects against many different viruses. It could be given immediately to vulnerable groups, such as older people and people with weakened immune systems, to prevent severe respiratory infection.

The biggest test will be whether the approach can deliver the same broad protection in people that it shows in the laboratory. If it can, it could change how quickly we respond to new respiratory viruses, giving scientists more time to develop targeted vaccines while helping protect people from the earliest days of an outbreak.

articles.title: Four ways to help your body adjust to the autumn time change
articles.author: Ronan Lordan, Postdoctoral Researcher in Circadian Biology, FutureNeuro Research Ireland Center & School of Pharmacy and Biomolecular Sciences, RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences
paras: An extra hour in bed sounds like a good deal. But while our phones may update to the autumn time change automatically, our body clock isn’t quite so quick. You may even find yourself waking up earlier than normal and ready for bed before your evening has properly begun.

The reason for this partly lies in our circadian system: the roughly 24-hour internal timing system that helps organise tiredness and alertness. Changing the time on a clock does not instantly reset that system.
But there are some things you can do to support your body clock in adapting to the time change. While these strategies won’t offer a guaranteed overnight reset, they will help you get back on track.
1. Dim the lights before bedtime

Your body doesn’t judge whether it’s day or night by using the numbers on a clock. Rather, a tiny region in the brain called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) – which acts as the body’s master clock – uses light signals from the eyes to help keep our circadian rhythm on track.

Bright evening light can suppress melatonin, a hormone that signals biological night, and shift your internal clock later. This can help explain why some people feel less sleepy at their usual bedtime during the long, bright evenings of summer.
But even the light from electronic devices such as phones or e-readers can contribute to melatonin suppression.

So as your intended bedtime approaches, switch to lower, softer lighting and reduce screen brightness. It’s recommended you keep light exposure low in the hours before bed and make the bedroom as dark as practical during sleep.

Of course, the autumn time change often means we’re tired before our usual bedtime as the early nights draw in. Shifting your body clock a little later can be helpful if you’re becoming sleepy and waking too early.
To do this, only start winding down before the bedtime you want. Don’t spend the entire evening in darkness as soon as the sun sets.

A walk, an outdoor lunch break or simply spending more of the day outside can strengthen the contrast between bright days and dim evenings. That contrast helps synchronise the circadian system, which evolved under a much stronger daily light–dark cycle than many indoor lifestyles provide.

When you get this daylight is important, however. Morning light generally moves the body clock earlier, while evening light generally pushes it later. That distinction matters when the clocks go back, because someone waking too early doesn’t necessarily need another signal to wake earlier.
After the clocks change, try to get daylight during your normal waking day rather than deliberately seeking bright light at an unusually early hour. A lunchtime walk is one practical option.

If early-evening sleepiness is the problem, spending time outdoors later in the afternoon, while daylight remains, may be better than prioritising first-thing morning light. In fact, a 2024 modelling study predicted that later-day light exposure could speed the autumn adjustment. However, the authors emphasised that these proposed interventions still need experimental verification.
Think of daylight as a useful daily cue – not a precisely proven clock-change prescription.
3. Stick to a regular sleep schedule
It’s tempting to treat the extra hour of sleep as permission to overhaul your weekend. But a regular routine is key.

Sleep depends on both the pressure that builds while you’re awake and the circadian signals that determine when you feel sleepy or alert. These processes interact, which is why sleep can’t always be summoned simply by deciding to go to bed.

Aim for reasonably consistent bedtimes and waking times according to the time change. Avoid swinging between very early nights, long lie-ins and late bedtimes. Keeping weekday and weekend schedules similar can support healthy sleep.
If you find that even with a consistent sleep schedule you’re struggling to fall asleep, choose a quiet activity done in low light until you feel ready for bed.

Dark autumn mornings can also make waking up feel harder. Keeping a broadly consistent waking time, getting morning daylight when possible and allowing enough time for sleep may help maintain a stable sleep–wake rhythm – although some grogginess immediately after waking is normal.
4. Re-think your afternoon coffee

The earlier nights that accompany the winter months can make it harder to get through the afternoon. When you feel groggy, coffee can look like the obvious solution. But as much as it pains me to give this advice as a coffee lover, you might want to skip that midday coffee.

Caffeine interferes with sleep long after its effects have worn off. A recent, small study found that a 400mg dose of caffeine (equivalent to around 3-5 cups of coffee) affected sleep even when consumed eight hours before bedtime. That’s quite a substantial dose, of course – and not one many of us are consuming in the mid-afternoon. Fortunately, the study also found that when a 100 mg dose of caffeine (equivalent to a single cup of coffee) was consumed four hours before bedtime, it had no effect on sleep compared to a placebo.

If sleep is difficult, moving your last caffeinated drink earlier and reducing the amount you drink are sensible things to try. Evening caffeine can also push the body clock later, so avoiding it may help when you’re trying to keep an earlier sleep schedule.

The autumn time change is a useful reminder that sleep depends on more than the number displayed on your phone’s clock. Most people adjust to the time change within a few days to about a week, although some can take longer. But if you’re still struggling a month later, the clock change may not be the whole story.

articles.title: Surviving cancer starts at diagnosis and continues after treatment – earlier survivorship care can help patients feel better and live longer
articles.author: Marci Lee Nilsen, Professor of Otolaryngology, University of Pittsburgh
paras: “You have cancer.” It’s a phrase that comes as a shock, then is quickly followed by a whirlwind of decisions that somehow feel fast and slow at the same time.

You have treatments to decide on. You are trying to figure out how you might work, care for your family and undergo a variety of intensive medical appointments all at the same time. You are centered on the here and now, and thinking about five or 10 years down the road is not at the forefront of your mind. Getting through treatment is the finish line you are reaching for; that is when you may actually feel like a cancer survivor.

As a nurse and scientist who has spent over a decade caring for cancer patients and studying ways to ease the effects of treatment, I have heard this story time and time again from both survivors and their loved ones. But survivorship actually begins at the time of diagnosis.

In fact, in our newly published research in JAMA Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery, my team and I found that patients with head and neck cancer who started survivorship care – healthcare services that support a cancer survivor’s physical, emotional, social and practical needs – earlier were more likely to stick to treatment and be alive without cancer three years after treatment.
What is cancer survivorship?

Clinicians and researchers consider a person a cancer survivor from the time they are diagnosed through the end of their life. More important than the term is what cancer survivorship is meant to look like for the patient.

Cancer survivorship reflects the patient’s experience with cancer and cancer treatment, and the physical, emotional and social effects that has on their life. Survivorship care is designed to identify and address the complex needs of a cancer survivor beyond just the physical changes. It involves coordinating care and promoting the person’s overall health and well-being.

This care can look different for each patient, depending on the cancer they have and their individual needs. For example, my team and I designed a survivorship clinic at UPMC in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to address the most common issues head and neck cancer survivors experience. In addition to surgeons and nurses, our team includes swallowing therapists, a physical therapist, a dental care team and a dietitian to help address issues with swallowing, nutrition, dental health, physical function and mood. All of these services are offered at the same location and can be completed in one visit on the same day, generally under one copay.

After the visit, the cancer survivor, their oncology team and their primary care clinician receive a care plan to help coordinate care and communication among all their providers. Rather than as a one-time session, our survivorship clinic builds relationships with survivors, supporting them as their needs change over time.
Timing matters for cancer survivorship

While a person becomes a survivor at the time of diagnosis, most survivorship care is delivered after the initial treatment has ended. This may be partly because to be accredited by a major medical body that sets cancer care standards, the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer, hospitals must offer at least three services to cancer survivors after they complete their initial treatment.
While survivorship care can ease physical and psychological issues after cancer treatment, survivors often report significant unmet needs before and during treatment.

In my specialty of head and neck cancers, many patients undergo a grueling five to seven weeks of radiation therapy, often in addition to chemotherapy. They experience a host of side effects: pain, mouth sores, skin burns, difficulty swallowing and weight loss, which together can lead to treatment interruption and hospitalization. These side effects often continue and sometimes worsen years after treatment.

While our survivorship clinic was initially designed for patients who completed treatment, we later expanded our services to patients before radiation. We previously found that starting survivorship care before radiation was associated with better quality of life and reduced symptoms.

In our newly published research, we found that among 471 cancer survivors, 62% of those who attended our survivorship clinic before completing radiation finished treatment on time, compared with 48% of those who were not seen before completing radiation. At three years, 60% of patients seen in the survivorship clinic before completing radiation were alive and cancer-free, compared with 39% of those not seen before completion. The association remained after accounting for whether patients completed radiation on time, suggesting that on-time completion may not fully explain the difference.

Although our results suggest that shifting the start of survivorship care to before treatment may improve outcomes, they do not prove it. Our team plans to test in a larger clinical trial whether starting survivorship care before radiation helps patients finish treatment on time and maintain quality of life, while also examining how teams coordinate care and referrals.
Survivorship care is not universal

Comprehensive cancer care implies not only a comprehensive treatment plan, but also supportive care that will help patients live well beyond their diagnosis and treatment. However, a 2024 survey of 384 facilities accredited by the American College of Surgeons Commission on Cancer found that only 1 in 5 programs estimated that most of their eligible patients receive survivorship care.

For head and neck cancer survivors specifically, nearly all clinicians routinely assess cancer recurrence, swallowing and thyroid function. But only about half address psychological symptoms, such as anxiety and depression, and fewer than 1 in 3 addressed body image or sleep problems.

Survivorship care is often framed as care that begins after treatment ends, which can delay patients’ access to support during treatment. Communication breakdowns may leave patients unaware of available services, while a lack of referrals can keep them from receiving needed care. Survivorship care also draws on clinicians with different areas of expertise, and some hospitals and treatment centers may lack enough dedicated staff time to provide a full range of services.
Thinking ahead in cancer care
The end of treatment is a huge milestone that patients and their loved ones reach for. But it is not where survivorship care truly starts.

Making survivorship care more accessible may help make cancer care more comprehensive. Clinicians and researchers can start planning for the survivor’s life after cancer even when it’s not on the patient’s mind. Bringing a team that combines treatment experts with rehabilitation and supportive care specialists into the room early can help achieve better outcomes for patients.
As a cancer survivor or a loved one, you don’t need to wait.

articles.title: Napoleon can be partly blamed for Gen Z’s weightlifting obsession – here’s why
articles.author: Claire Warden, Professor of Performance and Physical Culture, Loughborough University
paras: More than one quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than holidays or eating out.

Sport England data shows that Gen Z has begun to turn away from running, swimming and fitness classes towards gym and strength training. For them, weight training is seen as the best form of exercise because it can help build strength, improve appearance and boost overall health.

People have argued about the best forms of exercise for over two centuries. While today’s fitness trends tend to be more about improving the body and overall fitness, health has rarely been the sole reason why certain exercise trends gained popularity through the eras.
In 1806, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Prussia and, inadvertently, created the modern fitness industry.

As Napoleon’s troops stormed their way eastward, one Prussian man, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, began to seethe with anger. For Jahn, Prussian men had lost because they were physically weaker than the French.

The nation’s solution, according to Jahn, lay not in muskets – but muscles. So in 1811 Jahn opened a Turnplatz – an open-air gymnasium. Young men ran, jumped, climbed ropes, wrestled and vaulted. They also swung on two pieces of equipment that Jahn is believed to have invented: the parallel bars and the horizontal bar. Soon the trend spread to other nations, with England’s first outdoor gymnastics school opening in 1825.

The underlying logic behind Jahn’s Turnplatz system – that strong nations demanded physically strong troops – became a rallying cry for a wave of gymnastic and calisthenic systems for men and women across the century.

A popular form of entertainment in the Victorian era were strongmen shows, where muscular men would perform theatrical acts of strength. One of the most popular performers of the time was Charles “Samson” Sampson, whose act involved snapping chains with his chest.

But in 1889, a new kind of strongman arrived on the scene. During one of Sampson’s performances, a moustachioed strongman named Eugen Sandow stripped down to his pants in a London theatre, responding to a challenge from Sampson. But what made Sandow different from Sampson and other strongmen of the era was his physique. He was lean and sculpted.

From 1889 until his death in 1925, Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. He was deemed the “best specimen of manhood” by Harvard University physical educationalist Dudley Sargent. Sandow hosted the first major bodybuilding contest in London in 1901 and ran a health enterprise which spread across the British Empire, the Americas and Australasia. Thousands followed his mail-order courses, read his magazine and drank his cocoa.

Those lifting dumbbells and barbells to build their bodies like Sandow classed themselves as “physical culturists” in the same way that modern trainees may define themselves by Pilates, Hyrox or weight training.
Following Sandow and others, people trained for health but they also trained to become better workers, better spouses, to be more attractive or dynamic.
Although the state still mattered – Sandow even trained British troops for the second South African war – the emphasis slowly shifted to building the body for its own sake.
The post-war aerobics boom

The approach to exercise in the post-war era shifted due to an emerging new health concern: people were sitting down too much. This fear was fuelled by a 1953 work published by epidemiologist Jerry Morris which found that London bus drivers experienced higher instances of heart disease than conductors, who spent their day climbing stairs. The cause? Inactivity.

In the US, physicians began rallying against rising heart disease. Their radical solution was to advise people to run slowly for set periods of time – an activity we today call jogging. Pioneered in New Zealand and brought to the US in the 1960s, jogging soon kickstarted an “aerobics” boom.

New gym chains filled up with previously untrained enthusiasts running and doing aerobics classes. Aerobics classes were particularly popular with women. And in 1969, fitness instructor Jacki Sorenson originated the aerobics dance movement after she began setting routines to pop music, stitching together steps from jazz, folk, cha-cha and square dancing.
The popularity of aerobics only continued to grow throughout the 80s, thanks to actor Jane Fonda’s best-selling 1982 workout video which brought aerobics into the living room.

In 1977 the world was introduced to Austrian bodybuilder Arnold Schwarzenegger in the hit documentary Pumping Iron. Brash but charming, muscular but beautiful, Schwarzenegger and the entrepreneur pushing him, Joe Weider, popularised bodybuilding as we now understand it.
Pumping Iron hit cinemas at a time when aerobics had driven more people into gyms and new gym equipment made lifting weights far more accessible.

Schwarzenegger’s physique soon became a template for heroic figures in pop culture. Action stars, children’s toys and athletes all succumbed to the bodybuilding effect. Leading 80s megastar Sylvester Stallone even transformed his body with Schwarzenegger’s training partner Franco Columbu in preparation for Rambo and the Rocky movies.
Women were lifting, too. Lisa Lyon won the first women’s world bodybuilding championship in 1979. Two decades later women’s weightlifting reached the Olympics.

By the 2000s, lifting weights was no longer a fringe activity. Budget and 24-hour gyms were commonplace while sports such as CrossFit and powerlifting swelled with men and women. In recent years the hashtag #strongnotskinny has spread across Instagram and TikTok.

Exercise scientist Andrew Scott says that influencers have been a big part of this shift. None of this is new. Sandow sold his body on postcards and cocoa tins, Fonda sold hers on VHS and Schwarzenegger sold his at the cinema.
Once again, the world around us is changing how people move their bodies. Two hundred years ago, fitness served the country. Now it serves the algorithm.

articles.title: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs change how people eat, but nausea needs closer study
articles.author: Beverley O'Hara, Lecturer in Public Health Nutrition, Leeds Beckett University
paras: Someone taking a weight-loss drug might leave half their dinner because they feel comfortably full. They might also stop because they feel nauseous. Measuring the leftovers would reveal the same result, but tell researchers little about why the person stopped eating.

That distinction is important when studying how GLP-1-based medications, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, affect appetite. To understand changes in eating, researchers need to record nausea alongside hunger and fullness, including when it occurs and how severe it is.
Our new review found that studies rarely examined that relationship directly. This leaves uncertainty about how much nausea influenced particular measurements of appetite and food intake.

It does not mean these drugs work mainly by making people feel sick. Separate analyses of semaglutide and tirzepatide trials suggest gastrointestinal side effects, such as nausea and vomiting, explain only a small proportion of weight loss. But understanding people’s experience of eating during treatment requires more detailed measurements than many studies currently provide.
Why nausea needs closer attention

GLP-1 is a hormone released by the gut after eating. Medications that mimic its activity help regulate blood sugar and act on systems involved in appetite. They can also slow the movement of food out of the stomach. Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro, additionally mimics the activity of another hormone, GIP.

These medications can cause nausea, which may reduce someone’s desire to eat. Simply recording that a participant experienced nausea at some point during a trial cannot show whether it affected their eating when researchers measured it.

For that, researchers need to know when nausea occurred and how severe it was. Recording this alongside appetite and food intake could help distinguish feeling satisfied with less food from struggling to eat because of sickness.
Nausea could also lead participants to guess they are receiving the active drug rather than a placebo, a dummy treatment. That awareness might influence their answers to questions about appetite.

However, the limited evidence that directly examined nausea did not consistently suggest it explained changes in eating. One study found similar conclusions after excluding participants who experienced nausea or vomiting. Another found no association between nausea and reduced food intake.
The gap is therefore in understanding nausea’s contribution to particular eating measurements, rather than establishing it as the main explanation for weight loss.

Our review brought together 25 articles involving 4,060 participants, identified through searches conducted in November 2025. It focused on adults who were overweight or obese but did not have diabetes or other major health conditions. So its findings cannot automatically be extended to everyone taking these drugs.
We also conducted meta-analyses, which statistically combine results from comparable studies.
The clearest finding was that people taking GLP-1-based medications consumed fewer calories on average than those in comparison groups, although the size of the difference varied considerably.
Much of this evidence came from laboratory studies. Researchers provided meals and allowed participants to eat as much as they wished, then measured their intake.

These studies offer a controlled way to assess eating, but a laboratory meal cannot capture someone’s usual diet over weeks or months. Only two studies in the food-intake analysis used dietary recall, which asks people to remember what they ate. Those studies did not show a clear reduction relative to comparison groups.

That does not establish that the drugs fail to reduce everyday intake. Recalling food consumption accurately is difficult, and two studies provide limited evidence. It does mean that the size and persistence of changes outside the laboratory remain harder to establish.
The appetite analysis combined ten studies involving 321 participants. It found a small average increase in appetite suppression: around eight points on a 100-point scale.
Crucially, this analysis measured appetite after meals. It did not include fasting appetite or ratings covering a whole day or the previous week.

Participants marked how hungry or full they felt on a line, a measurement known as a visual analogue scale. These ratings are useful, but may miss changes between meals or in response to everyday situations.

The studies differed in their methods, and we rated the certainty of the appetite evidence as low. The findings cannot establish how strongly these drugs affect appetite throughout daily life, or how much this contributes to weight loss.
Several studies reported reduced food cravings or changes in food reward: how pleasurable or appealing someone finds food, and how strongly they want it.

These findings may overlap with reports of reduced “food noise”, a term describing persistent thoughts about food and urges to eat. Researchers have proposed a definition, but its measurement is still developing. Our review did not establish an overall effect on food noise.

Changes in food preferences were also inconsistent. Some studies found reduced liking or wanting for high-fat savoury foods and sweets. Others found broader reductions in interest, including in lower-fat or higher-protein options. Eating less does not necessarily mean eating a healthier diet.

A smaller meal can represent a welcome change for someone who previously struggled to feel satisfied. For someone experiencing nausea, it may reflect difficulty eating enough. Those experiences call for different kinds of support, even if both people are losing weight.

Following eating beyond the laboratory, while recording side effects consistently, would help researchers understand those differences. It could clarify how appetite changes over time and identify people who need help managing side effects or meeting their nutritional needs. Weight loss is an important outcome, but understanding how people feel when they eat would make the evidence more useful to those living with treatment.

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors: neuroscientist on whether you can really make someone yawn by faking it
articles.author: Stephen Jackson, Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience, University of Nottingham
paras: In the BBC reality show The Celebrity Traitors, the Traitors – James Acaster, Maya Jama and King Kenny – were set an unusual challenge: murder a Faithful by making them yawn. Their plan was to bore their target into yawning, then deliver the line “Am I boring you?” to seal the murder.

The task plays on one of yawning’s strangest features: its ability to spread from one person to another. Seeing someone yawn can be enough to trigger a yawn of your own, sometimes even when you are not tired. But would the same trick work if the yawn were deliberately faked?

Yawning is found across the animal kingdom and scientists believe that the behaviour dates back hundreds of millions of years. Humans yawn, but so do apes, dogs, horses, reptiles, birds and even fish, although contagious yawning – catching a yawn from another individual – is found in far fewer species.

Why do yawns spread, and what does this tell us about how we respond to other people? Researchers have several theories, from social bonding to the brain mechanisms involved in recognising and copying others’ actions. These may help explain whether a convincing fake yawn can fool us – and whether the Traitors’ task was as easy as it sounds.

One idea is known as the social bonding hypothesis. Humans and many social animals often copy each other’s behaviour without realising it. We mimic facial expressions, gestures, postures and even accents. This unconscious imitation can help strengthen social connections and create a sense of belonging.

Contagious yawning may be another example of this social mimicry. Studies have found that people are more likely to catch yawns from family members, friends and people they know well than from strangers. Similar patterns have been noted in other social animals. Wolves, for example, are more likely to respond to yawns from individuals with whom they have stronger social bonds.

Researchers have also reported that social status can influence contagious yawning. Individuals may be more responsive to members of their own group or to higher status group members, but responses are often weaker towards unfamiliar outsiders. This suggests that contagious yawning may reflect underlying social relationships.
Mirror neurons and mental simulation

A second theory focuses on the brain mechanisms that help us understand the behaviour of others. Some researchers have linked contagious yawning to the activity of so-called mirror neurons. These become active both when we perform an action and when we observe someone else performing the same action, and may help us understand the actions, intentions and feelings of other people.

According to this view, seeing somebody yawn effectively primes our own yawning system, making us more likely to yawn in response. A related idea is that contagious yawning may be linked to emotional contagion, the tendency to share the feelings and states of others. In this account, contagious yawning is related to empathy: our ability to understand and respond to another person’s experiences.

Several findings support this possibility. Contagious yawning typically emerges around the age of four or five years, roughly the same period when children develop more advanced abilities to understand what other people are thinking and feeling – often termed “mentalising”.

Reduced contagious yawning has been reported in people with autism and in those with psychopathic traits. However, while this finding fits the popular narrative for these conditions, the picture is not straightforward.

In autism, reduced contagious yawning may not necessarily reflect reduced empathy. Some studies suggest that differences in attention, particularly spending less time looking directly at faces and eyes, may account for much of the effect. In other words, if someone is not closely watching the yawner’s face, they may simply be less likely to detect the trigger for contagious yawning.
So, are fake yawns contagious?
The answer is “sometimes”, but less effectively than is the case for genuine yawns.

If contagious yawning depends partly on automatic social and emotional responses, then a convincing fake yawn may still trigger the same brain mechanisms as a real one. After all, the observer often responds to the appearance of a yawn rather than knowing whether it is genuine.

However, if the yawn looks obviously artificial or exaggerated, key social signals may be missing. The observer may not unconsciously simulate the action or interpret it as a genuine expression of another person’s state. As a result, the contagious effect may be weaker or absent.

In short, contagious yawning appears to be about more than simply seeing an open mouth. It may reflect social connection, shared attention and subtle emotional communication. For that reason, a fake yawn may be contagious when it looks authentic, but an obviously fake yawn is less likely to trigger the social mechanisms that make real yawns spread from person to person.

For the Traitors, that leaves a tricky question: could they make their target yawn without making it obvious that they were trying to do so? Their success depended on exploiting a behaviour that is partly automatic – but not entirely predictable.

articles.title: COVID inquiry: four ways to improve support for people with intellectual disabilities
articles.author: Richard Hastings, 125th Anniversary Chair, and Professor of Psychology Health and Social Care, University of Birmingham
paras: Anxiety. I always feel like I’m on edge. COVID, cost of living crisis, finances, current living arrangement. The majority don’t seem to care about COVID anymore and you can’t just ignore it, people are still dying from it.

Cara, whose name has been changed, described these concerns in our research into the continuing effects of the pandemic on people with intellectual disabilities. Her account shows how concerns about infection became entangled with uncertainty about everyday life.

The UK COVID-19 Inquiry’s care sector report, published on October 20 2026, focuses on how to improve support before another emergency. For people with intellectual disabilities, known as learning disabilities in the UK, that requires attention to how people live and the different kinds of support they need and receive.

The report’s first recommendation calls for pandemic planning at government, local and provider levels. But the formal recommendations are framed mainly in relation to care homes for older people and leave important details unspecified about how those plans should meet the needs of people with intellectual disabilities.

Our expert report to the inquiry, developed with input from people with intellectual disabilities and families, proposed more explicit commitments. These provide a starting point for addressing those gaps.
Protecting support for everyday life

People with intellectual disabilities have varied support needs. Our expert report describes most provision extends beyond residential care, including support for people living with family or in their own homes. Planning must also consider the services that help people participate in their communities.

Our study following adults through the pandemic found that access to day services had not returned to pre-pandemic levels by late 2022. Among adults interviewed directly, 37% had reported regularly attending before the pandemic; 26% were using some form of day service in the final research round.
These figures indicate why lifting restrictions did not necessarily restore people’s opportunities.
In our in-depth interviews, participants described losing independence and activities that were important to them. Future planning needs to address those consequences alongside infection control.

The inquiry’s first recommendation does not explicitly require protection of day services or community participation. In our expert report, we recommended planning to increase support during emergencies, while protecting access to community activities. Governments should explain how their response will achieve this.
Making health protection accessible
Public health advice is useful only if people can understand it and act on it.

Our expert recommendations called for information suitable for people with intellectual disabilities to be available at the same time as information for the general public. We also recommended prioritising the social care support people need to access healthcare, including vaccination.

The inquiry’s third recommendation requires accessible information about financial support schemes for care workers and providers. Its formal recommendations do not make an equivalent, explicit commitment to timely, accessible public health information for people with intellectual disabilities and their families.

Governments should build that requirement into pandemic plans. People with intellectual disabilities should help develop and test guidance before an emergency, with arrangements for updating it as advice changes.

Plans should also explain how people will receive practical help to follow that guidance or attend healthcare appointments. Publishing accessible advice cannot, by itself, resolve the loss of someone’s usual support.
Recognising intensive support needs

Families of people with profound and multiple intellectual disabilities described particularly difficult experiences in our research into their lives during the pandemic. They reported difficulties obtaining healthcare and support, alongside exhaustion and anxiety about the future.

The inquiry documents the loss of respite care and its consequences for unpaid carers. Yet its eight formal recommendations contain no dedicated requirement to maintain respite or other support for unpaid carers, or provide replacement care if a family carer becomes ill.

For people with profound and multiple intellectual disabilities, replacement support must be appropriate to their individual needs. Emergency arrangements should explain how someone’s care will continue if the people who usually support them become unavailable.

Our expert report recommended prioritising these individuals and their carers. Governments should make that priority explicit when implementing the inquiry’s planning recommendation, with resources to sustain support.
Including people outside existing services
Another gap concerns adults with intellectual disabilities who do not qualify for social care.

Our expert report called for better understanding of their lives and how their needs might increase during an emergency. Planning around existing social care recipients alone risks missing this large group.
Councils should work with people with intellectual disabilities and local organisations to establish accessible ways to seek help when circumstances change.
The How We Survive and Thrive commission, organised by Learning Disability England, has developed similar recommendations about maintaining support and involving people in decisions.

As governments implement the inquiry’s findings, people with intellectual disabilities and their families should help judge whether the resulting plans address their needs. Those plans must explain how support will remain available across different living arrangements, including for people who were managing without formal services before an emergency began.

articles.title: Has your fitness hit a plateau? An expert explains how to track progress and when to change your training plan
articles.author: Paul Hough, Lecturer Sport and Exercise Physiology, University of Westminster
paras: If you train regularly, your progress will eventually slow and personal bests will become harder to beat. When this happens, it’s tempting to start a completely new training programme – but this is usually the wrong move.
To understand why, it’s important to know how progress happens in the first place.

Exercise causes both immediate responses and long-term changes in your body. The body’s immediate responses to exercise are pretty obvious – an increased heart rate, breathing faster and your muscles feeling warmer. These short-term responses gradually settle back to normal after you finish training.

But when an exercise is repeated over weeks, the short-term responses we experience lead to longer-lasting physiological changes (called adaptations). These adaptations make the body stronger and more efficient. This is why a weight that once felt hard to lift feels easier after a few weeks or why you’re able to run a mile 30 seconds faster than you did a month ago.

If you continue doing the same training that produced your initial fitness gains, you can maintain the adaptations. However, over time, your progress will plateau because your body needs a greater training stimulus to drive further adaptations.
This gradual increase in the demands placed on your body is known as “progressive overload”. The increase can be small – such as adding a little weight or completing a couple more reps.
If you find your progress has stalled, the first question to ask yourself is whether you’re truly applying the principle of progressive overload. Here’s how you can figure this out.
If you do resistance training, record the weight, repetitions (reps) and sets you perform for each exercise at every session. This gives you a baseline to track your progress against.

At your next session, you can start applying progressive overload. Choose a rep range, such as eight to ten reps. Using your records as a guide, select a weight you can lift for eight reps with good technique, while feeling you could still manage another one or two reps.

Over the following sessions, gradually add reps using the same weight. Even one extra rep on one set is progress. When you can complete ten reps on every set with good technique, you are ready to increase the weight and drop the rep target back to eight.
This is known as double progression, because you progressively increase repetitions before increasing the weight. Increasing the reps before increasing the weight shows that you’re becoming stronger.
Progressive overload can also be applied to endurance exercise, such as running, cycling or swimming.

To start with, track your distances and pace to get a sense of where your fitness currently is. Progressive overload can then be applied by performing longer sessions, training more often or increasing your pace. It’s a good idea to increase only one of these at a time. This makes it easier to see what’s working and reduces injury risk.
A sensible rule of thumb is to limit your weekly increase in distance or time to no more than 10%. For example, if you usually run 25 miles per week, keep the weekly increase to about 2.5 miles.

You can track your progress by seeing whether you can cover the same distance in less time, or complete the same session at a lower heart rate or with less perceived effort. Improvements in any of these measures indicates that your fitness is improving.
If your progress stalls and you are not seeing small improvements, there are a couple of reasons why this may be happening.

Performance naturally fluctuates due to a range of factors including fatigue, stress, illness and lack of sleep. When this happens, doing more isn’t the answer. A large increase in training will only create more fatigue that will cause a drop off in performance. In extreme cases, this decline can take weeks or even months to recover from.

As a rule of thumb, if you’ve made no progress for three to four weeks, try doing an easy training week – sometimes called a “deload week”. This involves doing less training than usual to reduce accumulated fatigue. This can be done by doing fewer training sessions that week, or doing less during a session than you normally would do (such as half the number of sets you would usually complete, for example).
Athletes often do this before a major competition. If your performance returns to normal or gets better after a reduced training week, fatigue was the problem – not your programme.

But if progress has truly stalled after an easier week, try changing one thing at a time. This could involve swapping out one exercise or session in your training plan, rather than starting a completely new programme.

Consistency is important whether you’re training for a specific goal or you just want to improve your overall fitness. This is because adaptations happen when a specific exercise is done repeatedly under increasing demands.

Changing your training programme entirely makes it difficult to know if you’ve progressed because you can’t make a direct comparison. For example, if you swap your usual strength training session for a body pump class, you won’t know for sure if your strength has truly improved because the exercises and style of training are different.

Changing your programme becomes necessary is if you have a new goal or have experienced an injury. If boredom is the problem, consider changing how you train rather than what you train. For example, try doing shorter sessions, working with a personal trainer or updating your playlist.
So if you want to keep improving your fitness, don’t throw out your training plan at the first sign of a plateau.
